Duvo Raises $32 Million Series A to Become the One Platform Enterprises Run Their Operations On
October 14, 2026
Duvo
Duvo Raises $32 Million Series A to Become the One Platform Enterprises Run Their Operations On
PR Newswire
NEW YORK and LONDON, Oct. 14, 2026
Led by Balderton Capital, the round funds Duvo’s U.S. expansion. Its Enterprise Execution OS lets people and AI agents run processes together across the systems a company already has, starting with retail and consumer goods.
NEW YORK and LONDON , Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Duvo today announced a $32 million Series A led by Balderton Capital, with participation from existing investors Index Ventures, Northzone and Credo Ventures. The round brings Duvo’s total funding to $48 million and will fund its expansion, starting with retailers and CPG companies. Two executives lead the expansion. Michael Green joins from Databricks as Chief Commercial Officer. He previously served as a Senior Vice President at Salesforce. Spencer Insolia recently joined as Managing Director, U.S. He was previously President of Kmart and a Managing Director at Accenture.
Duvo is the Enterprise Execution OS: one platform where a company’s operations run, with governed processes and clear user approvals. Duvo is built so that AI in operations doesn’t stop at the pilot. Every process a company adds runs on the same connections, the same approval rules and the same record of results, instead of becoming another standalone project.
The platform works the same way for every process. Duvo Clarity captures how the work really runs, through AI-led discovery interviews with the people who do it, screen recordings and existing documents. Duvo’s agents then run the approved steps across ERPs, supplier portals, spreadsheets and inboxes, through APIs where they exist and through the same screens people use where they don’t. That’s why Duvo can be live in weeks with the first process without a small army of engineers or a major systems integration project.
Decisions and exceptions go to the person who owns them, and operating cockpits show what is waiting for a decision and what the process delivered. Most companies run on systems that don’t talk to each other, and the manual work in those gaps is where value leaks. Duvo runs that work on one platform and recovers the value.
Gartner projects spending on business orchestration and automation technologies will exceed $21 billion by 2029, as enterprises consolidate fragmented automation tools onto a single platform. But turning that into operational results is proving hard. Gartner predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. In a separate survey of 350 executives at companies with $1 billion or more in revenue, Gartner found that those reporting higher returns from AI agents and automation had cut staff about as often as those with modest or negative results.
“For a while I measured AI in heads, counting how many people an agent could replace. It’s the wrong unit,” said Tomáš Čupr, co-founder and CEO of Duvo and founder and Group CEO of Rohlik Group. “At Rohlik, the gains I’d point to came from work nobody had the hours for. Our planners used to check about eight at-risk products a day per market for shortages. Now every signal gets checked, around the clock. Optivolt Raises $32M Series A to Build the Brain for Solar Panels
October 21, 2026
Optivolt (Techstars 2018) has raised a $32M Series A to scale its Power Balancer, technology built into the solar panel that recovers energy lost to shade, dirt, and wear in real time. The funding will expand manufacturing and bring Optivolt to residential, commercial, and utility-scale projects, including ones that power AI data centers.
Optivolt (Techstars 2018) has raised a $32M Series A, bringing the company's total funding to $42M.
Optivolt builds power electronics that live inside the solar panel itself. Its core technology, the Power Balancer, helps panels produce more energy in the messy conditions they face every day, from shade and dirt to weather and uneven wear over time. The new funding will expand manufacturing and bring the technology to residential, commercial, and utility-scale projects, including installations built to power AI data centers.
Momentum Behind the Round
More than 20,000 solar panels with the Power Balancer have already shipped. Optivolt holds 19 issued patents with 27 more pending, and has earned UL certifications covering its junction box enclosure, panel-integrated electronics, rapid-shutdown system, and module safety.
The Problem With Today's Solar Panels
Solar has become one of the cheapest sources of new power. Still, a typical panel loses a meaningful share of its output whenever part of it is shaded, dirty, or wearing unevenly. Conventional panels rely on bypass diodes to route around underperforming cells, which protects the panel but leaves energy on the table. Many installers add separate optimizers or microinverters to recover some of that loss, adding hardware and cost to every system.
How the Power Balancer Works
The Power Balancer redistributes energy among groups of cells within a panel in real time. When one section is struggling, the system rebalances so the rest of the panel keeps producing. It replaces conventional bypass diodes and builds rapid shutdown and monitoring directly into the panel. Depending on the system design, that can reduce or remove the need for separate optimizers, microinverters, and rapid-shutdown devices.
Optivolt reports that the Power Balancer runs at 99.4% conversion efficiency under typical operating conditions. In the company's internal testing under defined shading scenarios, panels with its technology produced up to six times the power of panels using bolted-on optimizers.
What's Next
With the Series A closed, Optivolt will scale up production and speed deployment across residential, commercial, and utility-scale solar. Data centers are a growing focus, as demand for power from AI workloads continues to climb.
The People Building It
Optivolt was founded by Rohit Kalyanpur, a Thiel Fellow who has spent nine years rebuilding the solar panel from first principles.
"Solar became cheap enough to compete. I founded Optivolt to make it intelligent enough to power the world," said Rohit Kalyanpur, founder and CEO of Optivolt. "The result is the first solar panel system that thinks for itself... The next step is putting it everywhere."
To learn more, visit optivolt.com .

articles.title: Finance AI Tops Out at 51% on Due Diligence: Startup Raises $30M to Fix It
articles.snippet: Finance AI Tops Out at 51% on Due Diligence: Startup Raises $30M to Fix It Tech Times
articles.text:
By
Ryan Cook
Published: Oct 01 2026, 3:14 PM EDT
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share on LinkedIn
Share on Reddit
Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp
Alex MARTIN/AFP via Getty Images
The best artificial intelligence model in the world scores 51% on a realistic private-equity due-diligence simulation — and a nine-person San Francisco company just raised $30 million Series A to sell the labs responsible for those models the training infrastructure they need to improve.
Halluminate, founded in 2024 by CEO Jerry Wu and CTO Wyatt Marshall, announced a Series A led by Oak HC/FT on October 1, 2026, bringing the company's total funding to $38.5 million. Existing investors Y Combinator, Orange Collective, Heavybit, and FT Partners participated in the round, as did individual researchers from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta as angels — a customer list that doubles as a cap table.
What Finance Due Diligence Reveals About AI's Real Ceiling
In August, Halluminate published a benchmark it calls the Westworld Finance Diligence Bench — 88 tasks drawn from anonymized real private-equity transactions, written and reviewed by practicing deal professionals. Seven frontier models ran through it. The highest average score, across all seven models , was 51%.
That ceiling is worth examining closely. Halluminate designed the benchmark to simulate the complete body of work that a team of investment bankers, consultants, and accountants would produce together over several weeks: document review, contract analysis, evolving term sheets, and final deliverables. One benchmark task required an agent to redline a statement of work while navigating a 160-file data room, 21 emails across nine threads, and four sets of meeting notes — with deal terms changing throughout and certain provisions meant to remain fixed regardless.
Across the benchmark, agents consistently failed in the same ways: leaving out required changes, applying the wrong analytical method, or acting on information that had already been superseded. The failure wasn't in any single step. It was in carrying instructions through to the end — maintaining context and intent across a long, messy, real-world workflow.
These failure patterns are Halluminate's raw material. The company turns each identified breakdown into a reinforcement-learning environment: a structured, interactive simulation where a model can attempt the failing task, receive feedback, and iterate — without touching a real deal or a real data room.
Why Financial Work Is Harder to Simulate Than Code
The technical obstacle that makes finance-specific RL environments both more difficult to build and more valuable than their coding-domain equivalents comes down to a single engineering requirement: the reward function must be verifiable without a human reviewing every output.
Coding environments solve this cleanly. Run the code, check whether the tests pass. The outcome is binary and programmable. The reason OpenAI's reasoning models and Anthropic's Claude family improved so rapidly on coding benchmarks is that coding offers unlimited programmatic verifiability at the scale RL training requires — which can mean millions of individual task attempts per training run, according to Scale AI's analysis .
